comments.author: @SyAbna-s9v
comments.text:
Thank you for your interest in my island of Guadeloupe. I am pleasantly surprised that you have identified the major challenges my island faces on a daily basis.

I would also like to highlight the consequences of high youth unemployment and the rising levels of crime across the territory, as well as what I see as the French government's lack of genuine commitment to the development of its overseas territories since Guadeloupe became a department of France in 1946.

This situation is also linked to a long-standing policy of encouraging young people from the French overseas territories to migrate to mainland France. This policy dates back to the establishment of BUMIDOM in 1963, an organisation created to facilitate migration from overseas territories to mainland France. Many people believe that this policy contributed to the departure of young people from their home islands and helped ease social and economic pressures without adequately addressing their underlying causes.

For many Guadeloupeans, these issues raise fundamental questions about economic development, social justice, youth opportunities, and the future of our island. It is essential to understand this historical context in order to grasp the challenges Guadeloupe continues to face today.

replies.author: @LifewaysTravel
replies.text: Thank you for taking the time to add all of this context. 🙏 The connection between youth unemployment, migration to mainland France, BUMIDOM, and today's demographic and social challenges adds an important historical layer to understanding Guadeloupe. What really stands out is how decisions made decades ago can still shape families, opportunities, and the future of the island today. I truly appreciate you sharing this perspective from someone who knows and cares deeply about Guadeloupe. 🇬🇵❤️

replies.author: @SyAbna-s9v
replies.text:
Guadeloupe’s independence movement dates back to the 1960s, around the same period when many African countries were gaining their independence, and its roots go back even further. The issue is complex, but there have always been political groups in Guadeloupe advocating for independence, and some continue to do so today.

One has to understand that, from this perspective, France has little interest in allowing its overseas territories to develop too much economically, for fear that greater prosperity and self-sufficiency could strengthen their desire for independence. The idea is to maintain a delicate balance: allowing the population to live with a certain level of hardship, but not so much that it triggers widespread unrest, while avoiding too much development that could encourage greater autonomy and eventually lead to independence. In the long run, either extreme could fuel the independence movement.

replies.author: @LifewaysTravel
replies.text: That's a question people in Guadeloupe have debated for generations. The island's relationship with France is complex, and views on independence, autonomy, and remaining part of France are not all the same. Ultimately, the people of Guadeloupe should be the ones whose voices matter most in deciding their future. Thanks for raising such an important part of the conversation. 🙏

comments.author: @BenNguyen-u7m
comments.text: They call us "France’s forgotten island," but the harshest truth is that our own youth abandoned us first, leaving an entire generation of elders to wither away under the Caribbean sun

replies.author: @LifewaysTravel
replies.text: That’s an important point. The departure of younger generations didn’t happen in a vacuum, and understanding when that migration began, what opportunities or pressures drove it, and how policy shaped those choices adds a much deeper layer to Guadeloupe’s story. Thank you for bringing that historical perspective into the conversation. There’s clearly much more behind this issue than simply saying the youth chose to leave. 🙏

replies.author: @francissamuel8141
replies.text: One must know the genesis of the migration of the youths and when it started and How ard why it was encouraged and pushed. The history will surprise many.

replies.author: @LifewaysTravel
replies.text: That’s a powerful way to put it. When younger generations leave in search of work and opportunity, the loss isn’t only economic, it changes families, communities, and the future of the island itself. Thank you for adding such an important and deeply human perspective to the conversation. ❤️

comments.author: @HiddenUnrealPlanet
comments.text: Seen from above, the island resembles a butterfly, yet its two wings hold entirely different destinies: one side is a volcanic landscape of dense forests, while the other is a flat expanse geared toward tourism. Nature has dealt its cards with remarkable skill—crossing from one wing to the other feels as though you’ve stepped into an entirely different time zone.

comments.author: @CulturalTravel4K
comments.text: Grocery bills forty percent higher than Paris, aging water grids, and annual hurricane threats. Honest question: could your modern routine survive long-term living on Guadeloupe?

replies.author: @LifewaysTravel
replies.text: That’s an important perspective to add. Guadeloupe isn’t defined only by its challenges, and the island has its own agriculture, food production, culture, and strong local identity that deserve just as much attention. Thanks for bringing more balance to the conversation and sharing how you see Guadeloupe from the inside. 🇬🇵❤️

replies.author: @danielvirginie1431
replies.text: Yet, she is cheaper than the EC islands with very good quality food and clothing products. Guadeloupe also produce her own food produce and  her own industry (sugar, water, rum, food stuff, etc) Guadeloupe is a power house and is the most vocal island in the Caribbean and because of that has always been avoided by tourism or others who misunderstand her. Most of these surrounding EC islands when they are hit by natural disasters, Guadeloupe and Martinique are the ones who step in and pull them back up. But just like the French, she doesn't miss a beat and always keep the government on their toes😅Every situation in Guadeloupe is created to get a better solution😉
